standard_prerequisites.name: The map from identities to homotopies
standard_prerequisites.statement: There is a canonical map sending an identity of functions to the pointwise homotopy it induces.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the map whose being an equivalence is the conclusion, used at source lines 988 and 994.

standard_prerequisites.name: Equivalences and fibers
standard_prerequisites.statement: A map is an equivalence exactly when all its fibers are contractible, and a fiberwise map induces an equivalence on total spaces exactly when it is fiberwise an equivalence.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the reduction performed at source line 990 and the contractibility criterion used at source lines 995-999.

standard_prerequisites.name: Weak function extensionality
standard_prerequisites.statement: A product of contractible types over any index type is contractible.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the hypothesis applied at source line 1006.

standard_prerequisites.name: Retracts
standard_prerequisites.statement: If a type is a retract of a contractible type then it is contractible.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the step taken at source lines 1004-1006.

core_obligations: Unfold the conclusion so that it becomes the statement that the canonical map from identities of functions to homotopies is an equivalence for every family of types and every pair of sections (source lines 986-989).

Use that a fiberwise map induces an equivalence on total spaces exactly when it is fiberwise an equivalence, so that it suffices to show that the map induced on total spaces by the canonical map is an equivalence (source lines 990-994).

Observe that the total space on the left is the type of pairs of a section with an identity to the fixed section, which is contractible, so the goal becomes contractibility of the type of pairs of a section with a pointwise homotopy from the fixed section (source lines 995-999).

Identify the latter type, by the transposition result invoked in the proof, with a product over the index type of a Sigma type that is contractible in each fibre; record that the transposition result itself uses function extensionality for one of its composites, so without function extensionality only a retraction is available (source lines 1000-1005).
Conclude: the product is contractible by weak function extensionality, hence so is its retract, which gives the required equivalence and therefore function extensionality (source lines 1005-1006).

proof_roadmap.step: Reduce function extensionality to an equivalence statement about the canonical map on one pair of functions.
Pass to total spaces using the fiberwise criterion for equivalences.
Use contractibility of the left total space to reduce to one contractibility statement.
Transpose one-sidedly to a product of contractible types and conclude by weak function extensionality.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the labelled theorem wfetofe at source lines 980-983: weak function extensionality implies the full function extensionality axiom. The author's proof (source lines 985-1007) is a chain of reductions in which one link has to be weakened deliberately. Function extensionality is first reduced to the statement that the canonical map from identities of functions to homotopies induces an equivalence on total spaces (source lines 986-994); since the total space on the left is a type of pairs of a section with an identity, contractible by the characterisation of paths with one free endpoint, the goal becomes contractibility of the type of pairs of a section with a pointwise homotopy (source lines 995-999); transposing that type turns it into a product of contractible types, but the transposition result is proved using function extensionality for one of its two composites, so what survives is only a retraction, and the author records explicitly that a retract of a contractible type is contractible (source lines 1000-1006). The statement announces neither the retraction step nor the fact that the auxiliary transposition theorem has to be used one-sidedly.
